name: Amber Fort
label: Amber Fort
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Maota Lake' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Maota Lake' (relation/15961875): edge nearest the subject (739 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2591473: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Amber Fort' (409 m across).
notes: Hilltop Rajput fort-palace above Maota Lake.

text.description:
Amber Fort (also spelt Amer) sits high on a hillside above Maota Lake, and the lake is what makes the classic photo. The fort's ramparts, gates and cobbled paths climb the slope, and on a calm morning the whole thing is mirrored in the water below. Guides call that reflection the classic Amber image.

The palace is built of red sandstone and marble and laid out on four levels, each with its own courtyard. It was begun by Raja Man Singh and expanded by Jai Singh I in the early 1600s. Later rulers kept adding to it until the Kachwaha capital moved to Jaipur in 1727. The fort is part of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan, which became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013.

For a phone photo, the best spot is the eastern shore of the lake, below the fort, where you can fit the fort, the slope and the water into one frame. Arrive early, while the lake is still, and take a few frames. Even a light breeze breaks up the reflection. If you want a second angle, the viewpoints at Jaigarh Fort and along the Great Wall of Amer look back over the fort and the valley. Once inside the fort, look for the carved gates and latticed windows, which suit close-up shots.

Amer is about 11 km from Jaipur city, so allow time for the journey and for the climb up to the fort itself.
text.geographic_location: Amber Fort is in the town of Amer, about 11 km from central Jaipur, on a hill that juts into Maota Lake. The lake lies directly below the fort.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or station stops listed for this spot. Amer is about 11 km from central Jaipur, so check local transport options before you set out. Head for Maota Lake, below the fort. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fort and its reflection together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the water and want more of the shoreline. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the ramparts and gates.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Maota Lake (eastern shore of the lake, below the fort). The fort rising above the still lake, with its reflection in the water in calm morning light.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on a lower line, so the fort and its reflection fill the frame evenly and the horizon stays level. Keep the whole fort in view in one shot, then take a second, tighter shot with the telephoto on the ramparts. If you have time, a guide also suggests the road approaching the fort as another spot for the reflection. Jaigarh Fort and the Great Wall of Amer give high views back over the fort and valley.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fort to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky looks too bright. Hold your phone steady for a moment before each shot, and take several frames in case ripples spoil one. A Live Photo can help you pick the calmest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the water is still. One guide says the winter months, November to February, are best for the reflection.

text.access_note: Amber Fort itself has a paid entry ticket, while the lakeside viewpoint is outside it; check the official site before you go, and also check entry details for Jaigarh Fort if you plan to visit.
claims_not_in_sources: Facing west from the eastern shore in the morning, the sun is generally behind you, so the fort should be lit from the front.
Even a light breeze can break up the reflection in the water.
A telephoto lens compresses the view and helps pick out details of the ramparts and gates from a distance.

name: Hawa Mahal
label: Hawa Mahal
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Badi Chaupar' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Badi Chaupar' (node/8044083223): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/542886858: the OpenStreetMap point 'Hawa Mahal'.
notes: Pink sandstone façade with 953 small windows, best photographed from the street opposite.

text.description: The Hawa Mahal, or Palace of Winds, is a five-storey front of red and pink sandstone covered in small carved windows. Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh had it built in 1799, and it has 953 of these windows (called jharokhas). They were designed so that royal ladies could watch street life and festivals without being seen, and they also let cool air move through the building. It rises to about 15 metres, and the top three floors are only one room wide, so the whole thing looks like a pink honeycomb standing above the road. The most famous side is actually the back of the palace, which is part of why it photographs so well from the street: the pattern is bold, repeated and easy to read on a small screen. The best free shot is from the pavement at Badi Chaupar, on the opposite side of the road from the facade. From there you can fit the full front in one frame, with autos and pedestrians in the foreground to give a sense of scale. It is a busy junction, so wait for a gap in the traffic and keep to the pavement. If you want a higher, more head-on view, there is Wind View Cafe, which offers an elevated view, and a terrace by Rang Bihari Temple across the road. Cafe access can change and the temple stair entrance is hard to find, so confirm both on the map before you rely on them. Go early if you can: the facade faces east, so morning light falls directly on it.
text.geographic_location: The Hawa Mahal stands on the edge of the City Palace complex in the old Pink City of Jaipur. The best street-level view is from the Badi Chaupar crossroads, just to its south.
text.directions_text: There are no Metro or tram stops listed nearby, so use a map to reach the Badi Chaupar crossroads in Jaipur's Pink City. The Hawa Mahal is straight ahead to the north, about 2 minutes on foot away if you want to walk closer. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the pavement. If traffic or people force you to stand close, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit all five floors in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the windows and carving.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Badi Chaupar (pavement directly opposite the facade, northeast corner of the crossroads). The full honeycomb facade rising above the street, with autos and pedestrians in the foreground. The palace is to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines straight by holding the phone level. Wait for a gap in traffic so the whole front fits in one frame, and let a few people or autos into the bottom of the picture for scale. For a higher, more head-on view, Wind View Cafe or the terrace by Rang Bihari Temple are alternatives, but check access first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pink stone keeps its colour against the bright sky. If your phone offers Live Photos or motion, a few seconds of passing traffic can make a lively extra shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 8:00 AM, when the streets are quieter and the east-facing facade is lit directly.

text.access_note: The view from the street is free and open to anyone, but the palace interior and any cafe or terrace viewpoints may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Jal Mahal
label: Jal Mahal
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Amer Road' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Amer Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/134990320: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Lake Palace' (103 m across).
notes: Palace seemingly floating in Man Sagar Lake.

text.description: Jal Mahal, the Water Palace, sits in the middle of Man Sagar Lake, and that setting is why it photographs so well. Seen from the shore, a sandstone palace with pavilions on its roof appears to float on the water. It is built from local pink and red sandstone and has five storeys. When the lake is full, the lower four are underwater, so you only see the top floor, with its terrace garden and four octagonal domed pavilions (chhatris) at the corners. It was built around 1699 by Sawai Jai Singh as a duck-hunting lodge rather than a royal home. It was renovated and enlarged in the mid-18th century by Maharaja Madho Singh I. You can't go inside, so this is an outside-only stop, and a quick one. The best picture is the straight-on view from the lakeside promenade, directly opposite the palace, where the reflection fills the lower part of the frame. If you crouch low, the water takes up more of the picture and the palace seems to rest on its own mirror image. The hills behind the lake add a darker backdrop and make a good second shot. Give yourself time for both, but don't expect to stay long. Most of the picture is sky, water and one small building, so keep the composition simple and let the reflection do the work.
text.geographic_location: Jal Mahal stands in the middle of Man Sagar Lake in Jaipur, beside the road towards Amer (Amber). The royal cenotaphs of Gaitore are located opposite the lake.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop close by. Head to the lakeside promenade on Amer Road and go to its midpoint, where the palace is straight ahead across the water. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic straight-on view with the whole palace and its reflection. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter picture of the palace with the hills compressed behind it. The ultra-wide (0.5x) makes the palace look very small, so use it only if you want lots of sky and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Amer Road (lakeside promenade, midpoint, directly opposite the palace). A straight-on view of the palace floating on Man Sagar Lake, with its reflection filling the lower part of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch low and hold the phone close to the ground so the water reflection takes up the bottom half of the picture. Turn on gridlines and put the palace on the centre line so it and its reflection are balanced. For a different shot, move along the promenade to a spot where the Nahargarh hills rise behind the palace as a darker backdrop, which gives more depth and contrast.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the sandstone stays rich. Try a Live Photo, which may capture ripples on the water, and pick the stillest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the wind disturbs the water, gives the calmest reflection.

text.access_note: The palace itself is closed to visitors, so this is an exterior view from the public promenade; check the official site before you go for current access and any restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: Dragging the exposure slider down helps keep the sky from washing out.
A Live Photo may capture ripples on the water and lets you choose the stillest frame afterwards.
The palace looks small in an ultra-wide (0.5x) shot taken from the promenade.

name: City Palace, Jaipur
label: City Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Tattoo Cafe & Lounge' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'The Tattoo Cafe' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/455720627: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'City Palace' (312 m across).
notes: Royal palace complex with courtyards and ornate gates.

text.description: The City Palace is the royal residence of the Jaipur rulers, and part of it is still the home of the Jaipur royal family today. Sawai Jai Singh II began building it soon after he moved his court to Jaipur in 1727, and the main work was finished in 1732. It mixes Mughal and Rajput styles, and it now also houses a museum. For a phone photo, the useful point is that you do not have to go inside to get a good picture. From the rooftop of The Tattoo Cafe & Lounge you look out over the city, with the palace complex spread out below. That gives you the sweep of courtyards, pavilions and rooftops that is hard to see from street level. The pink-washed city around it is part of the picture. The colour is credited to Maharaja Ram Singh, who had the city painted pink to honour the visit of the Prince of Wales. If you do go into the ticketed palace, two spots are worth looking for. Pritam Niwas Chowk gives a close, symmetrical view of the richly coloured Peacock Gate. Jaleb Chowk shows the grand gateway with the Aravalli hills behind it. Either way, the palace can get crowded later in the morning, so an early start helps. Take a few wide shots for context, then a closer one of the palace buildings.
text.geographic_location: The City Palace is in the heart of old Jaipur, in the central north-east part of the city. The Virendra Pol, one of its visitor gates, is near Jantar Mantar. The rooftop viewpoint is in the Hawa Mahal area, a short walk south-east of the palace.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or similar stops near this spot, so head for the Hawa Mahal area in the old city. The Tattoo Cafe & Lounge is on a rooftop there, opposite the palace side of that area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the rooftop and the city in one frame. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the palace buildings, which sit some distance away. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the rooftop itself and the sky make up part of the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at The Tattoo Cafe & Lounge (rooftop, opposite the palace side of the Hawa Mahal area). A rooftop view over the city with the City Palace complex visible below, without going inside the palace. From here the photo looks over the city with the City Palace complex visible below, and you face north-west to find the palace.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the rooftops level. Place the palace buildings in the lower or middle part of the frame, with the sky and the city around them for scale. For a second picture, zoom in on one group of buildings. If you go inside the palace, the Peacock Gate at Pritam Niwas Chowk suits a straight-on, centred shot, and Jaleb Chowk suits a wide shot with the hills behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the palace to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. Take the shot at 1x first and the zoomed one after, so you have both.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early, because the palace gets crowded after about 10 AM.

text.access_note: The palace complex is ticketed and its photography rules vary, so check the official site before you go; the cafe rooftop is the free-access option, but check there too.

name: Nahargarh Fort
label: Nahargarh Fort
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Hilltop fort with sunset views over the city.

text.description: Nahargarh Fort sits on the edge of the Aravalli Hills, looking down over Jaipur. It was built mainly in 1734 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh as a retreat on the ridge above the city. With Amber Fort and Jaigarh Fort, it once formed a defensive ring around Jaipur, and walls ran across the hills to link the forts. The name means 'abode of tigers'. Local belief ties it to Nahar Singh Bhomia, whose spirit is said to have disturbed the building work until a temple was raised in his memory. The fort was extended in 1868, and a range of palaces was added in the 1880s and 1890s. Several films, including Rang De Basanti, Shuddh Desi Romance and Sonar Kella, were shot here. For a phone, the appeal is the mix of old stone walls, the hillside and the open sky. The fort is long and low rather than tall, so it suits a wide frame that shows the ridge it stands on. Use that distance to show the fort as part of the hillside rather than filling the frame with it. Keep the phone level, since the walls have strong horizontal lines. Check the official site before you go, as entry rules and closing times can change.
text.geographic_location: Nahargarh Fort is on the ridge of the Aravalli Hills above Jaipur, overlooking the city. It is one of the three hill forts, with Amber Fort and Jaigarh Fort, that once guarded Jaipur.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so plan your own way to the fort on the ridge above Jaipur. From there, face south to see the fort. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the fort and the hillside. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the walls do not fit in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out bastions, battlements or a stretch of wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. At that distance it will look fairly small in the default lens (1x), so zoom in a little or use the landscape around it to give it scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line of the walls along the lower or upper third, leaving room for sky or hillside. Keep the phone level so the long horizontal walls do not tilt. Try a 2x-3x shot that isolates the fort against the ridge, then a wider shot of the whole setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour. If the light is flat, a Live Photo can catch a moment of cloud or birds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on stone. Around midday, facing south, the fort may be backlit and the sky washed out.

text.access_note: The fort is a ticketed site with set opening and closing times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur
label: Jantar Mantar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vrihat Samrat Yantra' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Vrihat Samrat Yantra' (way/102878289): middle (60 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/102879535: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jantar Mantar' (247 m across).

text.description:
Jantar Mantar is an open-air observatory of 19 huge stone instruments, built by Sawai Jai Singh, the founder of Jaipur, and completed in 1734. The name comes from Sanskrit words meaning roughly 'calculating instrument'. UNESCO lists it as a World Heritage Site. For a phone photographer it works because the instruments are pure geometry: stairs, arcs, bowls and sharp shadows that look striking even in a quick snap.

The star of the visit is the Vrihat Samrat Yantra, the giant sundial. It stands 88 feet (27 m) high, and its face is angled at 27 degrees, the latitude of Jaipur. Its shadow creeps along at about 1 mm a second, roughly a hand's breadth every minute, so you can see it move while you line up a shot. A small cupola sits on top.

The classic picture is from the base, looking up the staircase towards the top. Two other good subjects are the Jai Prakash Yantra, a pair of hollow bowls with engraved lines, and the Ram Yantra, with its open stone cylinders. Leave yourself a few minutes to wander, because the angles change a lot from one instrument to the next. Mornings are the best time to come, as the light is warmer and the shadows are clearer.
text.geographic_location: Jantar Mantar is in central Jaipur, near City Palace and Hawa Mahal.
text.directions_text: Use a map app to navigate to Jantar Mantar, near City Palace. You can also start from City Palace or Hawa Mahal, both nearby. Once inside, head for the tallest structure, the giant sundial (Vrihat Samrat Yantra), and walk to the foot of its staircase. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the base of the sundial, so the whole staircase and the sky fit in. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the engraved scales and the cupola on top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (base of the giant sundial, facing up its staircase). The sundial's tall stepped face rising against the sky, with the staircase lines leading up to the gnomon. The middle of the site lies a little to the north-west of here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch a little, point the phone upwards and let the staircase lines run diagonally towards the top. Switch on the gridlines to keep the edges straight. For a change of subject, try the curved inside of the Jai Prakash Yantra bowl, shot across to the far side. The Ram Yantra gives clean parallel shadows across its floor.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so it stays blue and the stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as people often walk through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around 9 to 10 AM, when the light is warm and the shadows are long and clear. Afternoons are usually busier with tour groups.

text.access_note: Jantar Mantar is a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go for entry, opening times and photography rules.

name: Birla Mandir, Jaipur
label: Birla Mandir
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Birla Mandir' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/230927032: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Birla Mandir' (96 m across).
notes: White marble temple below Moti Dungri hill.

text.description: Birla Mandir, also called the Lakshmi Narayan Temple, is a white marble Hindu temple in Jaipur, dedicated to the goddess Lakshmi and to Vishnu (Narayan). It was built by the B.M. Birla Foundation and opened on 22 February 1988. It stands on a raised platform, with Moti Dungari hill behind it, and it has three towers. Marble figures on the outer walls include Christ, Buddha, Confucius and Socrates. It photographs well because the pale stone is clean and simple, the domes make a strong shape against the sky, and the grounds have gardens, steps and statues for closer shots. The founders, Rukmani Devi Birla and Braj Mohan Birla, are shown in covered pavilions facing the temple with hands folded. At night the temple is lit up. A lesser-known phone shot is the reflection pool just inside the entrance gate. On a windless day it can give a near-perfect mirror image of the main dome. Photography rules here are reported differently by different visitors. Most guides allow photos of the exterior, gardens and steps but not inside the prayer hall or sanctum, and some visitors say photos are banned even outside. Read the signs and ask a member of staff before you start shooting. If you can't use the pool, the wide view from Jawahar Lal Nehru Marg shows the whole façade with the hill rising behind.
text.geographic_location: Birla Mandir is in Jaipur's Tilak Nagar neighbourhood, at the foot of Moti Dungari hill. The temple sits just below the hill and its fort.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so check a map app for the best way to reach it. Look for Birla Mandir in Tilak Nagar, below Moti Dungari hill. The phone icon on the map is at the temple itself, at the reflection pool just inside the entrance gate. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the reflection in the pool. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) from Jawahar Lal Nehru Marg to fit the whole façade and the hill behind it. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the founders' statues and the carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand at Birla Mandir, at the reflection pool just inside the entrance gate. From here the main dome is ahead of you, and the pool shows it as a mirror-like reflection when the water is still.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the pool's edge on the lower third line, with the dome and its reflection filling the rest of the frame. Hold the phone low and close to the water to make the reflection larger. For a different view, take a wide shot from Jawahar Lal Nehru Marg, with the three domes in front and Moti Dungri Fort behind. The statues of the Birla couple at the B.M. Birla Family Museum also make a good human-scale shot. Moti Dungri Fort is privately owned, so it works only as a backdrop from below.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white marble keeps its detail. Wait for the ripples to settle before you press the shutter. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or rail to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a calm, windless day for the reflection. Evening is also a good time, when the temple is lit up. Check visiting hours on the day, as the complex is generally closed around midday.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship with its own photography rules, so check the signs, ask staff, and check visiting hours on the day.

photo.artist: Jean-Marc Astesana from Voisins le Bretonneux, France

name: Jaigarh Fort
label: Jaigarh Fort
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Fort on the Cheel ka Teela ridge above Amber Fort.

text.description: Jaigarh Fort sits on a rocky ridge of the Aravalli hills called Cheel ka Teela, the Hill of Eagles, looking down on Amer Fort and Maota Lake. It is also known as Victory Fort. The walls are thick and built of red sandstone, and the fort stretches about 3 km from north to south and about 1 km across. That makes it a long, strong shape against the sky, which is why it photographs well from a distance. Construction began around the middle of the eleventh century, and later rulers added to it. Jai Singh II built palace apartments here. The fort was also a cannon foundry, and it is home to the Jaivana cannon, which was once the largest cannon on wheels in the world. The fort stands roughly 400 m above Amer Fort, so views from inside look out over the hills and down on the palace below. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines so the long wall does not seem to tilt. Check the official site before you go for entry rules.
text.geographic_location: Jaigarh Fort is on the hills above Amer, about 10 km from Jaipur city. It stands high over Amer Fort and Maota Lake.
text.directions_text: The fort is near Amer, a short turn off the Jaipur–Delhi Highway. You can also climb to it from Amer Fort on a steep hill track. The phone icon on the map is about 170 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the fort on its ridge. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out ramparts and gateways. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move close inside the fort.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 170 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. The ridge and its walls will be in front of you at a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the ridge line on the lower third, leaving room for sky above. Use the telephoto lens to compress the walls and towers into a tighter picture. Keep any foreground hills or trees at the edges so they frame the fort rather than cover it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sandstone walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands when using telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit this view, as the sun would be behind you and light the walls with a warm tone. Midday haze can flatten the distant ridge.

text.access_note: Jaigarh Fort may be ticketed or have set visiting times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From a point west of the fort, afternoon sun would be behind the photographer and light the fort's walls.
Midday haze can flatten the view of a distant ridge.
The fort can be seen as a long wall along the ridge from the stand-here point.

name: Albert Hall Museum
label: Albert Hall Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ram Niwas Garden' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Ram Niwas Public Gardens' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1496872519: the OpenStreetMap point 'Albert Hall'.
notes: Indo-Saracenic museum, lovely when lit at night.

text.description: Albert Hall Museum is Rajasthan's state museum and the oldest museum in the state. It is a fine example of Indo-Saracenic architecture. It photographs well because the front is neat and symmetrical, with a central tower and dome and open garden space in front that gives you room to step back and fit it all in. The building was designed by Samuel Swinton Jacob and opened to the public in 1887. Its foundation stone was laid in 1876 during the visit of the Prince of Wales, later Edward VII, and the building is named after him. Inside, the collection grew from the crafts that Colonel Hendley gathered, and it now runs to thousands of objects, including paintings, carpets, jewellery and an Egyptian mummy. Go in the morning for soft light on the stonework, or in the evening once the building is lit. The garden is a public space, so the outside view costs nothing. A second option is to shoot the building from among the trees and lawns, with greenery in the foreground. A third is to look for its reflection in still water. Opening hours can vary, so check on the day before a night visit.
text.geographic_location: In Ram Niwas Garden, just outside the old city wall of Jaipur and opposite New Gate. It is on the edge of the walled city, with the garden around it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot. The museum stands opposite New Gate, inside Ram Niwas Garden, on the edge of the old walled city. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the whole symmetrical facade, with the garden in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the central tower and dome. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk much closer and want the full front in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Ram Niwas Garden (main front lawn, straight on from the central entrance, looking north). The full symmetrical facade with the central tower and dome, framed by the lawn in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the central tower up with the middle vertical line so both sides of the building match. Keep the phone level so the edges stay straight. Let the garden fill the bottom of the frame. If you have time, try the building among the trees, or its reflection in still water, as alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid, because the lit facade is much brighter than the sky around it. Phone photography inside the museum is free.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around 9-10 AM, for soft light on the stonework. In the evening, from about 7 PM, the facade is lit up. Opening hours can vary, so check on the day before a night visit.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the free public Ram Niwas Garden, but entry to the museum itself is a separate matter, so check the official site before you go.

name: Raj Mandir Cinema
label: Raj Mandir Cinema
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Raj Mandir Cinema' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7285323: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Raj Mandir is Jaipur's best-known cinema, and the outside is the part that suits a quick phone photo. The building has a rounded, meringue-like look in the Art Moderne style (sometimes called Streamline Moderne or late Art Deco), and it is framed against the street. Nine star shapes on the exterior stand for the nine gemstones of the Navaratna style, a nod to the jewellery house that owns and runs the cinema. It opened on 1 June 1976 and was designed by the architect W. M. Namjoshi. It was the last of the 34 cinema halls he designed. The cinema is on Bhagwan Das Road, near M.I. Road, and is often described as a symbol of Jaipur. It has also been called the largest single-screen theatre in Asia.

For a good photo, stand on the pavement at the street frontage and photograph the front facade in daylight. Keep the whole curved shape in view, with the stars and the street around it, so the picture shows where the building sits. The lobby is a different kind of picture: the chandeliers and grand staircase are worth a look if you are going to a show, though you should follow the cinema's rules about photography inside. Traffic and people pass the entrance all day, so wait a moment for a clearer gap before you take the shot.
text.geographic_location: Raj Mandir Cinema is on Bhagwan Das Road, close to M.I. Road, in Jaipur.
text.directions_text: Start from the M.I. Road area. From there the cinema is on Bhagwan Das Road, close by. From elsewhere in the city, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Raj Mandir Cinema on Bhagwan Das Road. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade as the eye sees it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the whole curved front in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a close-up of the star motifs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The picture shows the meringue-shaped Art Moderne exterior with its nine stars, set against the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the building straight so it does not lean. Include a little of the street to give a sense of place. If you go inside, the entrance hall with its chandeliers and grand staircase makes a second photo, shot before or after a show.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail. Indoors, try night mode for the lobby, and hold the phone steady against a wall or rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the exterior is clearly visible. Early in the day is likely to mean fewer people and less traffic.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the street, but the cinema is a working venue, so follow its rules about photos inside.

name: Galtaji
label: Galta Ji Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Galta Gate' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Galta Gate' (node/8042166840): point.
pin_note: Position from OSM N566816025 (Galtaji): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Temple complex in a hill gorge with sacred pools and monkeys.

text.description:
Galtaji is a temple complex tucked into a green valley in the hills at the edge of Jaipur. It photographs well because of the setting: temple buildings and hills fold into one another, and the view opens out toward the city. The most rewarding picture here is not of one building but of the whole valley.

The best place to start is near Galta Gate. Guides describe it as a valley viewpoint, and one reviewer says the walk up from the gate is the best way to experience the complex. The walking path and valley edge just beyond the gate give open views down the green Aravalli valley and across toward the city, with the temple complex's hills in the frame.

If you carry on, the Surya Mandir (Sun Temple) is reported to give a wide panorama over Jaipur's city and forts, with pink sandstone in the foreground. Expect steps and a climb of 15 to 20 minutes to reach it. The Lower Galta Kund, a sacred tank with temple walls and trees around it, is worth a few frames too, and the still water can give reflections.

Monkeys live here and can grab phones and food, so keep your phone secure between shots. Photography is generally allowed, but one guide warns of restrictions inside the temples, so look for signs before you raise your phone.
text.geographic_location: Galtaji is in the hills on the edge of Jaipur, in a valley setting away from the busy streets.
text.directions_text: From there the temple complex is about 1 km (955 m) to the east. Allow extra time if you climb on to the Sun Temple, as the climb is 15 to 20 minutes with steps. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of the valley, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view toward the city. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the temple buildings and hills in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Galta Gate (the walking path and valley edge just beyond the gate). Open views down the green Aravalli valley and across toward the city, with the temple complex's hills in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line so the valley fills most of the frame. Use the path or the edge of the gate as a foreground to give depth. For a different view, try the Surya Mandir for a wide panorama over the city and forts, with the pink sandstone in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the valley to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Panorama mode works well for the wide valley view if you turn slowly and keep the phone level. Keep a firm grip or a secure pocket nearby, as monkeys can grab phones.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning tends to give softer light, and it is sensible to avoid the hottest part of the day if you plan to climb.

text.access_note: This is a temple complex, so as a general courtesy dress respectfully, and expect some restrictions on photography inside the temples. Entry fees and hours can vary, so check on the day.

name: Sisodiya Rani Bagh
label: Sisodiya Rani Bagh
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sisodia Rani ka Bagh' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1181148520: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sisodiya Rani Bagh' (50 m across).
notes: Terraced Mughal-style garden with painted pavilions.

text.description:
Sisodiya Rani Bagh is a terraced Rajput garden, built in 1728 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II as a gift of love for his second queen. She came from the Sisodia Rajput line of Mewar, which is where the name comes from. The garden steps down in several levels, with fountains, watercourses and painted pavilions. A double-storeyed palace sits on the top terrace, with galleries and murals showing scenes from the life of Krishna.

For photographs, the quieter view is from the middle of the garden, in front of the water body. Here the water fills the foreground, and the fort and hills rise behind it. That layering gives a phone picture depth without any fuss. If you want the classic overview, the top terrace looks down over the tiers of the garden, and the painted Central Baradari pavilion makes a good close-up when low sun falls on its walls.

The fountains are often not running, so do not plan a shot around moving water. Aim for late afternoon, when you can catch both day and evening light. The garden is a ticketed site, so confirm entry fees and photography rules on the day. Check on the day whether tripods are allowed, and note that pre-wedding or professional shoots need permission from the Jaipur Development Authority.
text.geographic_location: Sisodiya Rani Bagh is about 6 kilometres from Jaipur city, on the Jaipur–Agra highway.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed close by. The garden is about 6 kilometres from Jaipur city on the Jaipur–Agra highway. Look for Sisodia Rani Garden and Palace. Once inside, walk to the middle of the garden to reach the phone icon on the map, in front of the water body. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the water, fort and hills together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the garden's edges, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the fort against the hills.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the water feature fills the foreground, with the fort and hills behind it. It is a quieter view than the one from the terrace.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the water along the lower third, with the fort and hills in the upper part. Crouch a little to bring the water closer to the lens. For a different angle, the top terrace gives a wide view down over the terraced garden with the palace in the foreground. The Central Baradari is good for a close shot of its painted walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fort to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps its colour. Try a quick Live Photo if the water is moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, around 4 to 5 pm, so you see the garden in both day and evening light.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed garden and palace, so confirm entry fees and photography rules on the day. Check on the day whether tripods are allowed, and note that pre-wedding or professional shoots need Jaipur Development Authority permission.

name: Moti Dungri
label: Moti Dungri
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Birla Mandir' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Birla Mandir' (way/230927032): middle (96 m across); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q28154167: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Hill with a palace-like fort and Ganesh temple.

text.description:
Moti Dungri is a Ganesha temple at the foot of a small hill, with a fort on top that is said to be modelled on a Scottish castle. The temple was built in 1761 under the supervision of Seth Jai Ram Paliwal, in the Nagara style, using limestone and marble. That mix of carved stone below and castle walls above is what makes the place so photogenic. The hill gives the scene a clear shape against the Jaipur skyline, so it works as a postcard-style view as well as a close-up of the temple.

From there you are far enough back to fit the hill, the temple and the fort into one frame. Then walk over to the temple itself for the carved exterior and the entry domes, with the fort rising behind. If you want a simple street-level shot, Moti Dungri Road gives a frontal view of the fort on its hill.

The fort is private and closed to visitors, so shoot it from outside. Photography inside the temple sanctum is restricted, and the rules for the courtyard seem to vary, so follow the signs and any staff instructions. A fair is held at the temple every Wednesday and it gets very crowded then. Come on another day if you want clear frames.
text.geographic_location: Moti Dungri is a temple complex in Jaipur, Rajasthan, at the foot of its own small hill. The Birla Mandir stands right next to it, to the south of the Ganesha temple.
text.directions_text: Moti Dungri is reached from central Jaipur, so check local access before you travel. The Birla Mandir and the Moti Dungri temple stand side by side. It is about 5 minutes on foot between the two. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full view of hill, temple and fort. Use the default lens (1x) for the temple front, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the fort walls on the hill.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Birla Mandir (elevated gardens). A wide-angle view of the Moti Dungri temple complex and the fort on the hill together, with the scale of the hill and its place in the Jaipur skyline. Check the view when you arrive, as the gardens are the only spot suggested for this wide shot. For a closer alternative, go to the Moti Dungri Ganesh Ji Temple for its carved stone exterior and entry domes with the fort behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the temple on the lower third, with the hill and fort filling the rest. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Moti Dungri Road gives a straight-on, street-level view of the fort as another option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hill or the fort to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out the stonework. Use the telephoto for the fort rather than cropping a wide shot afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone. Avoid Wednesdays if you want fewer people in your frame.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship with restricted photography in the sanctum, and the fort is private and closed to the public, so check the official site before you go, including for any camera fee.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit a hill, temple and fort into one frame from a short distance.
Walking time of about 5 minutes is calculated from the 281 m distance (281 x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).

name: Jagat Shiromani Temple, Amer
label: Jagat Shiromani Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jagat Shiromani Temple' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Sri Jagat Siromaniji Temple' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q21503605: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Carved marble temple in Amer town.

text.description:
Jagat Shiromani Temple is a 17th-century Hindu temple in the town of Amer, near Jaipur. Queen Kanakwati, wife of King Man Singh I, had it built between 1599 and 1608 in memory of their son Jagat Singh, who died young. It is dedicated to Krishna, Meera Bai and Vishnu, and it is one of the few temples in India where the poet-saint Meera Bai is enshrined beside Krishna.

For a phone photo, the star is the carved marble toran gate at the entrance. Its arch is flanked by elephant sculptures, and the pale marble stands out well against the sandstone of the temple. The stairs leading up to it let you shoot straight on or from a slight angle, which shows the depth of the carving and the elephants nicely. The temple is built mainly of locally quarried sandstone and marble, with carved deities, musicians and floral patterns on the walls, so close-up detail shots are worth taking too.

From the courtyard you can look back up at the arch, with Amer Fort rising behind it, which makes a good second picture. Keep your photos to the architecture and be respectful: avoid photographing worshippers or the inner sanctum. Monkeys are around, so keep your phone secure in your hand when you are not shooting. Go early if you can, as the gate is quieter and the facade has its best light.
text.geographic_location: In the town of Amer, near Jaipur, behind Amer Fort on the Sagar Road side (Devisinghpura).
text.directions_text: Check local options for getting to Amer and head for the Sagar Road side, behind Amer Fort. The address is Sagar Rd, Devisinghpura, Amer. Once you are in the town, the temple entrance and its marble gate are the obvious place to start. Panna Meena Ka Kund is about a five-minute walk away if you want a second stop. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the marble gate head-on. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you can't fit the whole arch in, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the elephants and the carvings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front of the marble toran gate, at the foot of the entrance stairs). The carved marble arch flanked by elephant sculptures, framed head-on as the temple's main entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the arch up with the middle vertical line so the gate looks balanced. Then step slightly to one side on the stairs for an angled shot of the elephants. For a second picture, go up into the courtyard and look back at the arch with Amer Fort rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white marble to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the carving stays crisp and doesn't wash out. Use 2x-3x for the carving details instead of zooming in further. Portrait mode is not needed here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the sandstone facade has the best light and the gate is quietest.

text.access_note: Entry to the temple is usually free, but check on arrival whether photography inside is free. It is a place of worship, so dress modestly and avoid photographing worshippers or the inner sanctum.

name: Badi Chaupar
label: Badi Chaupar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Badi Chaupar' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Badi Chaupar' (node/8044083223): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q25203214: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Large square in the Pink City facing Hawa Mahal.

text.description:
Badi Chaupar, the name means "Large Square", is the big open crossroads in the busy market part of Jaipur. It is also known as Manak Chowk. It is one of the two major squares built by the King of Amer, and Tripolia Bazar, the city's central market, runs between it and its smaller sister, Chhoti Chaupar. The area is still a hub for artisans, jewellers and craftsmen, so there is plenty of street life.

For a phone photo, the draw is the view across the square. From the pavement opposite the Hawa Mahal you see the palace's honeycomb facade rising above the buses, rickshaws and traffic. Guides call this the classic free street-level view. The facade tends to draw the eye more than the square itself, so decide which you want before you raise the phone.

Traffic and overhead wires can get in the way. Be patient and wait for a gap in the vehicles, and keep to the pavement while you do. Early morning, around 8-9am, is the calmest time and the best light on the facade, as the Hawa Mahal closes after sunset. If you want a higher angle, the rooftop Wind View Cafe looks across the square at the full five-storey facade. Photography there may be for customers only and the rules can change, so ask before you go up.
text.geographic_location: Badi Chaupar is in the old market area of Jaipur, at one end of Tripolia Bazar, the city's central market. It sits on the crossroads facing the Hawa Mahal, with Chhoti Chaupar as the other major square nearby.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Tripolia Bazar, Jaipur's central market, and head for Badi Chaupar, one of the two squares that mark the bazaar. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, navigate to Badi Chaupar or the Hawa Mahal on your phone map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Hawa Mahal facade above the traffic. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and the street in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the facade's windows and leave out wires.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Badi Chaupar (pavement opposite the Hawa Mahal facade, facing north-west). The open crossroads square with the Hawa Mahal's honeycomb facade rising above the traffic, buses and rickshaws in the foreground. The middle of the square lies a little to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the facade straight against the vertical lines. Leave the buses and rickshaws in the foreground to give a sense of scale. Wait for a gap in the traffic before you press the shutter. For a higher view across the square, Wind View Cafe is an alternative, but it shows the palace more than the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. In a busy scene, try Live Photos or motion so you can pick the best frame from the moving traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around 8-9am, before the square gets crowded and while the facade has good light.

text.access_note: Badi Chaupar is a public city square, open to everyone, so take care with the traffic; for the Hawa Mahal and the cafe rooftop, check the official site or ask the staff before you go.

name: Kanak Vrindavan
label: Kanak Vrindavan
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kanak Vrindavan' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q12417933: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Garden complex with temples near Jal Mahal.

text.description:
Kanak Vrindavan is a terraced garden in a green valley below Nahargarh hill, on the road towards Amer Fort. It was commissioned by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh roughly 275 years ago as a place of recreation for the royal household. It is named after the Vrindavan of Krishna's stories, and 'Kanak' comes from one of the Maharanis, Kanakde. Today it is managed by the Government of Rajasthan.

For photographs, the garden gives you several things in one visit: lawns and trees, a series of fountains, marble decoration, and the Govind Deoji temple with its mirror and jali work. The best view is from the upper terraces, which face Jal Mahal and Man Sagar Lake. The fountains and marble work sit in the foreground, the lake lies below, and the Aravalli hills rise behind. Guides rate it as a better place for a clear view of Jal Mahal than the main road. The main garden is divided into eight sections, with a main fountain called Parikrama carved from a single slab of marble, so there is plenty to frame without walking far.

If you have time, the Radha Madhav Temple is a good second subject, with its facade and mirror and jali work set among greenery and carved stone. Walk slowly, look for a clean foreground such as a fountain edge or a carved arch, and keep the lake and hills as the backdrop.
text.geographic_location: Kanak Vrindavan lies in the valley at the foot of Nahargarh hill, approximately 8 kilometres north of Jaipur, on the way to Amer Fort. Jaigarh Fort and Nahargarh Fort are close by.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, metro or tram stops for this spot, so head north from Jaipur towards Amer Fort. The garden is roughly 8 kilometres north of Jaipur, beside the road to Amer. Look for Kanak Vrindavan along that road. Once inside, the phone icon on the map is on the upper terraces. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the terraces and fountains. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit fountain, lake and hills into one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Jal Mahal on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the fountains and marble work are in the foreground, with Jal Mahal and the lake below and the Aravalli hills behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put a fountain or a piece of marble work low in the frame, then let the eye run on to Jal Mahal and the hills beyond. Turn on gridlines and place the lake on a third line. If you also visit the Radha Madhav Temple, take a straight-on shot of the facade and a close one of the mirror and jali work.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on Jal Mahal to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the water and stone. Live Photos can catch the moving fountains.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or golden hour, when the stone glows. Mornings are also good for softer light.

text.access_note: This is a government-managed garden and temple complex, so entry and photography rules may apply; check the official site before you go.

name: Rambagh Palace, Jaipur
label: Rambagh Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rambagh Palace' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Taj Rambagh Palace' (way/397085651): edge nearest the subject (732 m across).

notes: Former royal residence, now a luxury hotel with gardens.

text.description: Rambagh Palace is a pale pink sandstone palace with marble detail, set in about 47 acres of gardens on the southern side of Jaipur. It began in 1835 as a modest garden house. By 1925 it had grown into the main home of Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II, and after independence it became India's first luxury palace hotel. Taj Hotels has run it since 1972. It photographs well because the roofline is so busy: domes, cupolas and chhatris stand out against the sky, and the long arched verandahs and carved balconies give you plenty of repeating shapes. Open lawns in front let you step back and take in the whole frontage. On one side, Moti Dungri Fort can be seen behind the grounds. Peacocks roam the lawns, so keep your phone ready for a bird walking across the foreground. Take a wide shot of the whole façade first, then move in on the rooftop details. If you have time, the verandah and the formal gardens, with their fountains and lawns, make good second pictures. The palace is a working hotel, so it is best to treat the photos as a visit to someone's grounds: be quiet, keep to the public areas and follow any staff instructions.
text.geographic_location: Rambagh Palace stands south of Jaipur's old walled city, on Bhawani Singh Road, about 8 km outside the city walls. It sits in its own large gardens.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops to give you a starting point, so head south from Jaipur's old walled city towards Bhawani Singh Road, by taxi or hired scooter. The palace is about 8 km outside the city walls. Ask your driver for Rambagh Palace and its main gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full façade and lawn, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the domes, cupolas and chhatris against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front and side façade, from the palace lawns). The palace's domes, cupolas and chhatris framed against the sky, with the lawns in the foreground and Moti Dungri Fort visible in the background on one side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the roofline on the upper line so the domes have sky around them. Keep a strip of lawn in the foreground to give a sense of scale, and wait for a peacock to walk through if one appears. For a different view, try the verandah's arched frontage or the formal gardens, if you are allowed in.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the pink sandstone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the stone does not wash out. Use the telephoto for the roofline details.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, according to one guide. Peacocks are often seen in the evening light.

text.access_note: Rambagh Palace is a private, working luxury hotel, so access to the grounds, the lawns and the verandah may depend on a booking or a visit as a guest or diner; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens helps fit the whole width of the façade into one picture from the lawn.
Lowering the exposure slightly helps keep the sky blue against pale stone.
A taxi or hired scooter is the practical way to reach the palace from the old city.

text.description: Govind Dev Ji is a Hindu temple dedicated to Radha and Krishna, set inside the City Palace complex in Jaipur. Maharaja Jai Singh II, who founded the city, brought the deities from Vrindavan in the 18th century. The deity was installed in a building in gardens behind his palace, and a permanent temple was built there later. For a phone photo, the draw is the temple's sandstone and marble exterior with green garden planting around it, which gives you a calm, colourful frame in a busy part of the city. Its Satsang Hall also holds a Guinness World Record, awarded in 2009, as the world's widest concrete building. It has a single roof span of 119 feet with no pillars, but this is an interior feature, so don't expect to photograph it from outside. Photography of the main deity and inside the sanctum is prohibited, and the rules for the outer halls and gardens are described differently in different places, so ask staff on site before you raise your phone. The garden is the safest open-air place to start. Take a wide first shot of the whole building, then move closer for details such as carved stonework and the colour contrast between stone and leaves. Keep your phone away from worshippers' faces and be discreet during prayer times.
text.geographic_location: Govind Dev Ji Temple stands within the City Palace complex in Jaipur, Rajasthan. The garden around it lies behind and beside the temple building.
text.directions_text: No listed railway, Underground or tram stop is near the temple, so check local transport options to the City Palace complex in Jaipur. The temple is inside the complex, and Jalebi Chowk is the square from which its entrance area is approached. Once inside, follow signs or ask staff for the way to the temple and to Jai Niwas Garden. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the temple with the garden around it. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved details and the stone's texture without walking up to the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jai Niwas Garden (garden around the temple, behind/beside the temple building). The temple's sandstone and marble exterior, framed by the surrounding green garden. This open-air spot is the safest place to take photos.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the temple's vertical lines straight against them. In the garden, use trees and planting at the edges of the frame to make a natural border. If you want a second angle, Jalebi Chowk shows the entrance area and approach to the temple within the City Palace complex.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down slightly so the pale marble keeps its detail. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) only if you can't fit the building in, and keep the camera level to avoid leaning walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone. Temple prayer times vary, so confirm them locally if you want to see the temple at its busiest or quietest.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship inside the City Palace complex, so check the official site before you go for access, entry arrangements and photography rules.
